name: Simone Weil
role: French philosopher, mystic and labour activist (1909–1943)
summary: Weil began on the left as a trade-union activist and critic of Marx, and moved toward a Christian-inflected philosophy of obligation. She held that obligations to human beings come before rights, that the soul has needs such as order, liberty, obedience, equality, hierarchy and rootedness, and that political parties and totalitarian states poison thought. She opposed colonialism and the pursuit of national prestige, and wanted property widely held and work made meaningful.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: She wants the police honoured and the whole penal apparatus, police and courts included, treated as solemn and sacred, and criticises their discredit.

alienated-labor.rationale: The Encyclopedia reports her view that modern industry's orders and speed and its division of labour reduce workers to cogs who cannot think in their work.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: She rejects 'art for art's sake' as a shield for writers whose books shape conduct, would punish or discredit them, and favours repressing press and radio for vulgarity and a corrupting moral atmosphere, while keeping a reserve of absolute freedom for pure thought.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: She argued against French colonial rule and described colonial conquest as destroying subject peoples' cultures and honour.

class-struggle-history.rationale: She says Marx merely pasted the label 'class struggle' on facts of the soul's craving for liberty and power and left out war, an equally important factor, so there is no Marxist interpretation of history.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: She wrote against French colonisation of Indochina and against French claims to Morocco and Tunisia, and held that force destroys the values and cultures of colonised peoples.

consent-of-governed.rationale: She makes obedience rest on consent given once for all, not on fear of punishment or hope of reward, and says rule by constraint deprives masses of the consent that gives authority its basis.

death-penalty.rationale: She says the penal system must awaken a sense of justice in the criminal through pain or, where fitting, even by death.

decide-locally.rationale: She wants intense local and regional life, and calls progressive decentralisation of social life the only salvation, though doubting it can come from the centre.

democracy-best.rationale: She says democracy and majority rule are not good in themselves, only means to goodness; the unjust will of a whole nation is no better than a tyrant's, and she gives a Weimar-style majority persecuting Jews as the example.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: She holds that the republic as it stood was not a democracy, because voters never get the means to express judgment on public questions and are subject to officially inflamed collective passions, so elections alone do not make it one.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: She argues that a proletariat deprived of force cannot take command by a coup, and that Marx's premises on the state should have led him to foresee the totalitarian state, not to endorse proletarian rule.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Her book opens by saying the notion of obligation takes precedence over right, and that only obligation can be unconditional.

experts-over-public.rationale: She criticised the closed knowledge and caste privileges of specialists as feeding oppression, and wanted workers to think and understand their labour.

independent-unions.rationale: She says unions die when turned into single compulsory official bodies and hopes real unions can again express worker thought and honour, with legal influence over the official bodies.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: She says a man placed at the head of society for life must be a symbol and not a chief, 'as is the case for the king of England', and accepts that arrangement.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: She calls the money-driven system unhealthy and says Marxism supplies a totalitarian state with its doctrines, so neither offers a sound basis.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: She treats feeding the hungry as an eternal obligation: someone with food in abundance who passes a starving person at the door without giving is not innocent.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: She says a head of state for life must be a symbol, not a chief, limited by convention more than anyone, and she wants public life without parties.

one-party-rule.rationale: She calls the single party the extreme degree of evil and the inevitable end of party struggle, and calls for public life without parties.

participatory-democracy.rationale: She holds that taking initiative and responsibility in decisions touching others is a vital need, and that a collectivity denying it must be transformed.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: She forbids discipline binding members of groups of ideas and holds that a group with opinions tends to impose them on members, damaging thought.

person-over-state.rationale: She says collectivities are owed respect as food for souls but are not above the human being, even where sacrifice is demanded.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: She says each collectivity, patrie included, is unique and irreplaceable, and the sole organ preserving the spiritual treasures of the dead for the living and unborn.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: She judges property legitimate only insofar as it is real, that is, insofar as it meets the need for property that all people share; ownership that satisfies no one's need is 'null'.

religions-one-truth.rationale: She says the morality coming from mystic thought is one in all authentic traditions, reflecting one absolute good outside the world, while religions mix it with social morality.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: She says publications meant to influence conduct must harm no one illegitimately and must never deny the eternal obligations toward the human being once law recognises them.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: She suggests forbidding professional organisations from calling strikes, permitting unions to do so with reserves, forbidding coercion and protecting continuity of economic life.

sacred-nation.rationale: She writes that there is no holy nation, only Christ is truth, and that a collectivity is owed respect as nourishment for souls, not for its own sake.

single-common-good.rationale: Her 'general will' is the convergence of individual reasoned judgments on what is just and in the public interest, made without the pressure of collective passion or party groups.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: She says any collectivity governed by a sovereign chief who is accountable to no one is in the hands of a sick man.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Her programme is built on the needs of the soul and a civilization grounded in the spirituality of labour as what politics should serve.

total-state.rationale: She names the totalitarian systems an abyss the French fell into, and says the totalitarian idol is merely painted red instead of brown.

universal-morality.rationale: She holds that obligation to the human being is eternal and confirmed by the universal conscience, and that the morality from mystic thought is one and unchanging across Egypt, Greece, India, China and Christianity.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: She says positive rights that contradict the eternal obligation are stripped of legitimacy exactly to that extent, and she reserves the demands of conscience from obedience.

vanguard-party.rationale: She argues for abolishing all parties, and says totalitarian parties are forged through exclusions for opinion, so she rejects a disciplined revolutionary party.

war-builds-character.rationale: She argued that wars are conflicts with no definable objective and that the policy of prestige means war, to be avoided; force dehumanises those who wield and those who suffer it.

widespread-small-property.rationale: In 'La propriété privée' she calls private property a vital need of the soul and wants most people to own their home, a little land and, where technically possible, their tools.

workers-own-party.rationale: She proposes abolishing every political party, workers' ones included; the workers' movement should express itself through unions and open circles of ideas.

notes: Themes searched: government (parties, democracy, head of state), liberty (expression, punishment), economy (property, unions), world (war, colonialism), society (obligation, nation). Read in full: the Stanford entry, the parties essay, the London fragment on Marx, and Part 1 plus sampled passages of L'Enracinement. Many statements (health care, tax, trade, immigration, gender and others) have no recorded position.
